translation: Vervaeke’s fourfold map of knowing: propositional, procedural, perspectival, and participatory. The point is that cognition is not exhausted by explicit beliefs or facts.
origin_background: This is Vervaeke’s umbrella taxonomy, but it is not made from nothing. Propositional and procedural clearly inherit the older knowing-that / knowing-how distinction, while perspectival and participatory draw on phenomenology, ecological psychology, and embodied or enactive cognitive science. The exact synthesis is distinctively his, but the ingredients are older.
vervaeke_usage: He uses the 4Ps to argue that modern people often overvalue propositional knowledge and underappreciate the forms of knowing that actually reorient attention, skill, identity, and world-disclosure.

translation: Knowing that something is the case: explicit beliefs, claims, statements, and descriptions that can be said or judged true or false.
origin_background: This is the most familiar philosophical sense of knowledge in analytic epistemology: knowing-that. Vervaeke inherits the label from that broader tradition rather than inventing it from scratch.
vervaeke_usage: He treats it as indispensable but insufficient. You can have lots of propositions without having the skill, orientation, or transformation needed to live wisely.
source_note_title: Manual corpus enrichment — Vervaeke core frameworks
notes: Added to support the 4Ps cluster explicitly.

translation: Knowing how to do something: skill, fluent competence, and embodied performance rather than merely stating the right rules.
origin_background: It is closely related to the classic knowing-how distinction, especially foregrounded by Gilbert Ryle against the idea that all intelligence reduces to explicit propositions or inner rule books.
vervaeke_usage: Vervaeke uses it for the trained performance dimension of cognition: what you can reliably do or enact even when you cannot fully state all the rules that guide you.
source_note_title: Manual corpus enrichment — Vervaeke core frameworks
notes: Added to support the 4Ps cluster explicitly.

translation: Knowing from a situated point of view: a felt orientation in which some things show up as salient, dangerous, inviting, or relevant before you explicitly theorize about them.
origin_background: This is not a single famous inherited label in the way knowing-that and knowing-how are. It is better understood as a synthesis of themes from phenomenology, ecological psychology, and situated cognition: how the world shows up from within a lived perspective.
vervaeke_usage: He uses it for the salience-shaping, orientation-setting dimension of cognition: the way a situation is already framed for you before deliberate reflection begins.
source_note_title: Manual corpus enrichment — Vervaeke core frameworks
notes: Added to support the 4Ps cluster explicitly; origin background is interpretive rather than a single canonical source label.

translation: Knowing by being involved in a way that changes both you and what can show up for you. It is not just observing from outside but being transformed through engagement.
origin_background: Vervaeke’s usage resonates with embodied, ecological, and enactive approaches to cognition, plus older philosophical themes about transformation in the knower. It is less a single inherited technical term than a synthesis of those traditions.
vervaeke_usage: He uses it for the deepest mode of knowing: the form in which identity, attention, and world-disclosure are reshaped together through participation rather than detached spectatorship.

translation: The family of approaches that say mind is not just brain-bound symbol processing, but embodied, embedded, enactive, and extended.
origin_background: The 4E umbrella became common as philosophers and cognitive scientists grouped together several anti-brain-bound approaches. Major background sources include Varela, Thompson, and Rosch’s The Embodied Mind (1991) for enactive and embodied themes, and Clark and Chalmers’s The Extended Mind (1998) for the extended-cognition strand.
vervaeke_usage: Vervaeke often works inside this broader post-cognitivist space, especially when stressing that cognition is enacted through body, environment, skill, and participatory sense-making rather than only inner representation.

notes: Added because the app should expose the wider cognitive-science lineage around Vervaeke’s terminology.

translation: The idea that cognition is shaped by the body’s sensorimotor capacities, not just by abstract computation inside the brain.
origin_background: Embodied approaches push back against a purely disembodied view of mind. A major landmark in the later history is Varela, Thompson, and Rosch’s The Embodied Mind (1991), though the broader background also draws from phenomenology and ecological psychology.
vervaeke_usage: Vervaeke leans on this when he treats intelligence as inseparable from skill, salience, and situated action rather than as mere manipulation of detached propositions.
source_note_title: Manual corpus enrichment — 4E cognitive science background

translation: The idea that thinking is inseparable from the environment and niche in which an organism is acting; cognition is shaped by worldly scaffolds, not just inner states.
origin_background: The embedded strand of post-cognitivist cognitive science stresses organism-environment coupling and problem solving in real situations. It is part of the broader 4E family rather than a doctrine with one single canonical founding text.
vervaeke_usage: This matters for Vervaeke whenever cognition is treated as world-involving and context-sensitive rather than sealed inside a private inner theater.
source_note_title: Manual corpus enrichment — 4E cognitive science background
notes: Added for the 4E cluster; origin background is intentionally broader than a one-paper citation.

translation: The view that cognition is not passive mirroring but active sense-making: organisms bring forth meaningful worlds through embodied interaction.
origin_background: The enactive approach is strongly associated with Francisco Varela, Evan Thompson, and Eleanor Rosch, especially The Embodied Mind (1991), where cognition is framed as embodied action and world-enacting sense-making.
vervaeke_usage: This is one of the clearest background lineages for Vervaeke’s talk about relevance realization, participatory knowing, and the co-shaping of self and world.
source_note_title: Manual corpus enrichment — 4E cognitive science background

translation: The claim that cognitive processes can sometimes extend beyond the skull into reliable external supports such as tools, symbols, notebooks, or other scaffolds.
origin_background: This strand is strongly linked to Andy Clark and David Chalmers’s paper The Extended Mind (1998), which argued that under the right conditions external structures can count as part of a cognitive process rather than as mere aids to it.
vervaeke_usage: Even when Vervaeke is not explicitly arguing for the strongest extended-mind thesis, the background matters because his framework treats cognition as scaffolded by practices, environments, and cultural machinery rather than just by inner representation.
